newsitem.title: JAMAICA: Jamaica's coffee board in the red - government.
newsitem.headline: Jamaica's coffee board in the red - government.

text.p: KINGSTON, Jamaica, April 7, Reuter - A Jamaican government study has found that its state run Coffee Industry Board (CIB) is J$2 billion (US$57.14 million) in debt, an amount roughly equivalent to two years of coffee exports.

The government-commissioned study of the sector released Monday found a number of local coffee farms are not viable and should be shut down. In addition, farmers owe the CIB J$118 million (US$3.37 million) in unpaid loans disbursed through the board.

On March 24, angry coffee farmers converged on the CIB's Kingston offices, claiming they had not been paid for deliveries made to the board. The board is responsible for supervising the buying of all ripe beans in an effort to preserve the quality of Jamaican coffee. The board also has responsibility of marketing the coffee abroad.
The report stated that many of the board's problems stem from the fact that not only does it regulate the sector, it grows coffee on its own account.
The study revealed the CIB has still not repaid a US$7.8 million loan from several Japanese buyers, provided to help rehabilitate coffee farms after Hurricane Gilbert struck in 1988.
Only US$1.7 million of the loan was disbursed to farmers. The remainder was kept by the CIB to upgrade its own farms.

The CIB's board of directors are themselves all major coffee farmers, creating conflicts of interest and as a result, the study said, "the decisions that emanate are those of the members who are the most influential or who can shout the loudest."

The study, carried out by a team of Jamaicans from the public and private sectors, recommended that the CIB divest its farming operations and separate its regulatory, marketing and processing divisions into distinct operational units.
The report also recommended that government write-off the CIB's J$2 billion in capital debt, as most of it is government- guaranteed and "cannot be repaid by the CIB or the coffee industry."
Earlier this year, one major private coffee processing plant was put into "friendly" receivership after it was unable to service its loans.

Jamaica's famous Blue Mountain coffee currently fetches US$9-12 per pound on the world market, while its high mountain coffee sells for US$6-8 per pound, well above the US$1 per pound now prevailing for Brazilian and Colombian beans.

In addition, industry analysts have long pointed out the country could triple its coffee production of some 15,000 tonnes per annum and still not meet world demand. The Japanese are the largest buyers of Jamaican coffee.
